# Ticket: # 1365617 - Comcast's injection of notifications into browsing content is a phishing risk 

Date: 12/23/2016 1:20:31 PM 

City/State/Zip: Ann Arbor, Michigan 48104 

Company Complaining About: Comcast 

_____________________________________________________________________________ 

# Description 

This month I went over my Comcast data cap, and Comcast modified several HTTP web pages I visited, to inject an in-page notification about my data usage. 

This might seem like a customer-friendly feature, bu t it’s dangerous for Comcast’s users. This 

practice will train customers to expect that their ISP sends them critical messages by injecting them into random webpages as they browse. Moreover, these notifications can plausibly contain important calls to act ion which involve logging into the customer’s Comcast account and which might ask for 

financial information. 

Any website could present its users an in-page dialog which looks similar to these Comcast alerts. 

The notification’s content could be entirely controlled by criminals hoping to harvest users’ Comcast account login information. This would give an attacker access to users’ email, which is a gateway to reset the user’s passwords on most other sites — remember, most password recovery mechanisms revolve around access to an email account. 

I have previously complained about this, and a Comcast “Customer Security Assurance Technician 2” acknowledged that this is a risk. The company’s continued injection of content into pages like this 

demonstrates a lack of concern for their users’ security. 

Finally, in responses to complaints about this, Comcast often points to RFC 6108 in an attempt to make this practice seem more legitimate. It is important to note that RFC 6108 is simply an informational memo publishe d by Comcast, it specifically “is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.” This document has no value in defending the 

practice. _____________________________________________________________________________

Over the past few months I've had problems with my apple devices, which after speaking with Apple support, seems that it may be due to someone accessing my Apple ID. 

I have asked if I can view a log of when my account was accessed. The first intrusion I believe happened on 9/21/16 during the afternoon/ evening. 

On 12/19/16 I received a notice from Apple that someone tried to recover my password for my yahoo account /Apple ID, which unfortunately is broadcast on the phone instead of allowing just a user name (leaving the actual email address private). 

After this I tried resetting my Apple ID password. I selected a new password but when I immediately tried to log in with it, I was told it was incorrect. I was at home using a secure wifi connection. I am fussing the problem originated at the Apple server. The 2 step verification would not work as advertised, but I did manage to get one of my other devices to display a verification code ( manually because the one that was supposed to come from Apple did not show up on any of my devices. 

More recently I tried to reset the password again, ~ 12/22/16. I answered the questions, gave a phone number for verification and received an automated call from Apple stating they would call me "in a few days with instructions on how to reset my password." I called Apple support yesterday, 12/26/16, and the representative stated this was not the the common practice for Apple (calling someone back with instructions). 

I think the 2 step verification gives a false sense of security because it has not worked properly. Also having a full email address displayed on your phone in the Apple ID settings makes it easier for the account to be compromised and it appears to be no measures in place to track when the account is being accessed. There also appears (for me at least) an ususual number of "cannot connect to the server" errors. Yesterday I was talking on the phone, they sent me a code and when I click on it, it takes me to the Apple ID website but "error, cannot be verified, no server connection." It was not a lack of Internet connection. I was talking on the phone and using cellular Internet. If I had no service the call would have dropped.... _____________________________________________________________________________
